title: NoSQL & Distributed Data
summary: When one database can't hold your data or take your traffic, you spread it across many machines. NoSQL is the family built from day one to do that — trading joins and strict schemas for scale and survival.

blocks.markdown:
NoSQL is what you reach for when one machine can no longer hold your data or take your writes.

- **"Not Only SQL"** — drops some relational rules (strict schema, joins, cross-row ACID) to win horizontal scale.
- Built on **two ideas**: **partitioning** (split data so it fits and spreads load) and **replication** (copy data so you survive failures).
- It is **not "better than SQL"** — just a different point on the trade-off curve.
- You trade away convenience to buy scale and resilience, paying for it with more work in the app.

blocks.subTitle: Which model to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Pick the model whose cheap operation matches your hottest query.

| You need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Fast lookup by exact key | Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) |
| Query inside nested records | Document (MongoDB) |
| Huge write volume, time-series | Wide-column (Cassandra) |
| Relationship traversal | Graph (Neo4j) |
| Cross-row transactions, joins | Stay relational |

blocks.subTitle: The four data families
blocks.markdown:
Every NoSQL store is, at heart, a choice of data model.

- **Key-value** — a distributed hash map. `put`/`get` by exact key, value is opaque. Fastest, but no "find all users in Mumbai."
- **Document** — values are queryable JSON; filter and index on inner fields, flexible schema. Great for hierarchical records read together.
- **Wide-column** — sparse sorted rows, each with different columns. Tuned for massive writes and range scans; no joins.
- **Graph** — nodes and edges as first-class. Cheap relationship traversal, but hard to shard cleanly.

blocks.subTitle: Partitioning: who holds the key
blocks.markdown:
A **partition** (shard) is a subset of data on one node-group. The partitioning function decides which key goes where.

![Hash versus range sharding](assets/nosql-distributed-data/hash-vs-range-sharding.svg)

- **Hash partitioning** — `hash(key)` picks the partition. Even load, but adjacent keys scatter, so range scans hit every node.
- **Range partitioning** — sorted contiguous ranges per node. Cheap range scans, but writing "now" all day creates a **hot partition**.
- Fix a hot range with a **compound key** — prefix the timestamp with something high-cardinality.

blocks.subTitle: Replication: surviving failure
blocks.markdown:
Each partition is copied onto `N` nodes (the **replication factor**, usually 3) so a node can die without losing data.

![Leader-follower versus leaderless replication](assets/nosql-distributed-data/leader-follower-vs-leaderless.svg)

- **Leader-follower** — one leader takes all writes; followers replicate and serve reads. Simple, but followers **lag** and failover risks split brain.
- **Multi-leader** — several writers (often one per region); needs conflict resolution.
- **Leaderless** (Dynamo) — any replica takes writes, conflicts resolved on read. Stays available, no single writer to lose.

blocks.subTitle: Quorums: consistency without a leader
blocks.markdown:
In a leaderless system, the quorum rule keeps reads fresh with arithmetic.

![Quorum read and write with R plus W greater than N](assets/nosql-distributed-data/quorum-read-write.svg)

- Write to `W` replicas, read from `R`, out of `N`. If **`R + W > N`**, the read-set and write-set must overlap by one node.
- That overlapping node holds the latest write, so the read can't miss it — you keep the newest version.
- `R=1, W=N` for fast reads; `W=1, R=N` for fast writes; **`R=W=(N+1)/2`** for balance.
- It's strong-ish, not fully linearizable.

assets.alt: Quorum read and write with R plus W greater than N

blocks.subTitle: Pattern: query-first table design
blocks.markdown:
In wide-column stores you model the table around the read, not the entity — there are no joins.

```sql
CREATE TABLE messages_by_chat (
  chat_id    text,        -- PARTITION KEY: all of a chat together
  message_id timeuuid,     -- CLUSTERING KEY: sorts newest-first
  sender_id  text,
  body       text,
  PRIMARY KEY (chat_id, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);
```

- "Latest 50 in chat C" is a **single-partition** sequential read — no scatter-gather.
- A megagroup makes one partition huge: bucket the key as `(chat_id, day)` to cap its size.

blocks.subTitle: The core tensions
blocks.markdown:
Every distributed-data choice reduces to a handful of tensions.

| Tension | What you trade |
|---|---|
| Consistency vs availability | Refuse writes, or diverge and merge |
| Even load vs range scans | Spread keys, or scan them cheaply |
| Write vs read speed | LSM eats writes, pays on reads |
| Normalize vs denormalize | One copy + joins, or duplicate + fast reads |

CAP only bites *during* a partition; the rest of the time you tune latency vs consistency with `R`/`W`.

blocks.subTitle: Decision rules
blocks.markdown:
Match the store to your dominant access pattern.

- **Fetch one thing by known key** → key-value or document.
- **Huge append-heavy writes** (events, metrics, logs) → wide-column; design the partition key for spread.
- **Questions about relationships and depth** → graph database.
- **Multi-row transactions, ad-hoc joins, strong consistency by default** → stay relational ([relational-db-internals](relational-db-internals)).
- Many "we need NoSQL" instincts are really "we need an index" or "we need a read replica."

blocks.subTitle: Two systems to know cold
blocks.markdown:
Two databases anchor most interview answers.

- **Cassandra** — wide-column + **leaderless**. Consistent hashing, tunable `R`/`W` per query (`ONE`, `QUORUM`, `ALL`), and an **LSM-tree**: writes append to a commit log plus memtable, flush to immutable SSTables, merge via **compaction**. Eats writes; you model per query and denormalize.
- **MongoDB** — document + **leader-follower**. Each shard is a replica set with one primary and auto-election on failure. Shards by hash or range on a **shard key** — pick it badly and you get a hot shard. Has multi-document ACID since v4.0.

blocks.subTitle: Keeping replicas in sync
blocks.markdown:
Leaderless replicas drift apart, so two background mechanisms pull them back together.

- **Read repair** — when a read notices a stale replica, it writes the fresh value back.
- **Anti-entropy** — a background process compares replicas (often via **Merkle trees** to find differing ranges cheaply) and syncs them.
- A failed quorum write isn't rolled back: replicas that accepted it keep it, so it may still surface later. Treat failed writes as "unknown outcome" and retry idempotently.
- See [consistency-replication](consistency-replication) for the full treatment.

blocks.subTitle: What to monitor
blocks.markdown:
Distributed stores fail quietly until they don't. Watch for:

- **Per-node / per-partition load skew** → a hot partition; your key choice is failing.
- **p99 latency, not averages** → a struggling replica or compaction storm hides in the tail.
- **Replication lag or pending repairs** → reads going stale; a failover would lose more data.
- **"Could not achieve QUORUM"** → enough replicas down that writes are failing — an incident in progress.
- **Compaction backlog and disk growth** → writes outrunning compaction; reads climb and disks fill.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production:

- **"No schema means no data design."** The opposite — modeling moves into your app, and you design tables around queries up front.
- **"NoSQL is faster than SQL."** Only at the operations it's tuned for; slower or impossible at joins and ad-hoc queries.
- **"Higher replication factor = stronger consistency."** No — `N` is durability; consistency comes from `R`/`W`. `N=5` with `R+W ≤ N` still reads stale.
- **"Adding nodes rebalances evenly."** Only with a high-cardinality key; a bad key keeps the hot partition on one node.
- **"Denormalization is a hack."** In NoSQL it's the intended design — the discipline is fanning out the updates.
